pairs.rationale: The earlier departure narrates the disciples entering a boat and setting out while Jesus had not yet come to them. The crowd's later observation looks back to that departure without Him. This internal back-reference preserves the crowd's additional single-boat observation and does not add an actual boarding statement to6:21's willingness to receive Jesus.

Jesus explicitly interprets this crowd's seeking as motivated by having eaten the loaves and been filled. This links the narrated search with His later assessment, rather than a generic travel comparison. The motive is attributed to Jesus' reported words and is not independently inferred for every person or for another crowd.

The crowd asks when Jesus arrived, whereas the reader has already received the evening departure, encounter upon the sea and the boat's immediate arrival narrative. This is a specific contrast between narrated travel knowledge and the crowd's question, not Jesus' spoken travel explanation or a newly calculated clock time.

Peter's reply to the question about leaving names Jesus' words of eternal life and the group's confession; Jesus then qualifies the Twelve's position by speaking of one devil, identified as Judas. This explains the narrative response without asserting every individual had Peter's faith or predicting that no disciple would depart.

Both episodes discuss going into Judea in relation to Jesus' work and the disciples. Here His brothers urge the trip so disciples see His works; later Jesus proposes going and speaks of the disciples' believing in the Lazarus setting. Speakers, purpose and danger differ; neither is made the same journey or a proof of the brothers' private motives.

The hearers speculate that Jesus might go to the Greek Dispersion and teach Greeks; later Greek visitors approach through Philip and Andrew to seek Jesus. This contrasts imagined outward travel with visitors approaching Him. It does not narrate the speculated journey, identify the two groups or claim the later requested audience is explicitly reported as granted.

The Galilee-prophet objection to Nicodemus is compared with Nathanael's earlier objection about good coming from Nazareth and Philip's invitation to come and see. Both challenge a claim through regional origin. The places and addressees are not conflated, and the comparison does not independently disprove the Galilee claim by assigning a prophet modern geographic coordinates.

The reported caught-in-adultery charge is compared with the legal case of a man found lying with another man's wife. Deuteronomy explicitly concerns both parties and death; this unit does not specify stoning. The comparison supplies legal offense background without inventing the woman's marital details, the absent man's fate or an additional verdict on her case.

The earlier preserved instruction tells the sinless person to throw first; the later narration marks the departure as occurring when they heard. This supplies the actual spoken antecedent without adding a conscience clause, stating each accuser's inner guilt or explaining why the older ones left first.

Both identity demands receive a reply challenging the hearers' reception of Jesus' speech. John8 preserves Why do I even speak to you at all; John10 says He told them and they do not believe, adding the witness of works. The first reply is not replaced by a familiar from-the-beginning rendering.

Both healed beggars become objects of public identity recognition. John reports disagreement and the man's own identification; Acts says the people recognized the former alms-seeker now walking and praising God. The disabilities, responses and individuals differ, and the ordinary I am he is not equated with Jesus' distinct identity sayings.

Both healed men are questioned about Jesus, with different limits of knowledge. John5 says the healed man did not know who it was; John9 has already named Jesus but does not know where He is. This sharpens the reported who/where difference without inventing broader ignorance, lack of faith or an escape method.

The parents affirm that this is their son, born blind, but say they do not know how he sees or who opened his eyes and refer the questioners to him. This answer distinguishes their certified identity and former blindness from their stated limits concerning the healing, without deciding an unstated private degree of knowledge.

The narrator explicitly relates the parents' response to fear of synagogue exclusion, then repeats their referral to their adult son. This stated explanation contextualizes their limited-knowledge answer without declaring that they lied, changing their reported knowledge or assigning the same response to every parent.

Jesus later connects His absence at Lazarus's death with the disciples' believing. That explicit comment illuminates the absence within the earlier delay narrative. It does not state the arithmetic of the two-day stay, prove when Lazarus died relative to the message, or supply an unstated lack of love.

Both locate Bethany in relation to Jerusalem: John explicitly calls it near Jerusalem and gives about fifteen stadia; Luke names it with Bethphage by the Mount of Olives as Jesus goes toward Jerusalem. This geographical comparison does not independently verify the distance, fix coordinates or equate it with a Sabbath-day journey.

The reference to where Martha had met Jesus looks back to her earlier going to meet Him while Mary remained in the house. This distinguishes the two sisters' meetings within the narrative. The earlier unit does not independently measure Jesus' position or repeat the later statement that He had not entered the village.

Both scenes combine weeping with a question about where a body has been laid. Jesus asks about Lazarus and receives a come-and-see answer; Magdalene seeks where Jesus has been laid while not recognizing Him. The speakers and bodies differ, and neither Mary is identified with the other or either question made proof of an unstated limit of divine knowledge.

The council invokes the Romans as a threat to their place and nation if belief spreads; the Passion scene invokes Caesar while pressuring Pilate, and the chief priests profess Caesar as king. This compares explicit Roman political arguments around Jesus without verifying the council's prediction, defining place as one compulsory referent or equating every participant.

Andrew and Philip mediate the request to Jesus here; earlier Andrew brings Simon and Philip tells Nathanael about Jesus and invites him to see. The named disciples' mediating roles recur, but the persons and actions differ. The comparison does not assert that the Greeks' requested audience occurs or supply the motive for Philip consulting Andrew.

The Psalm explicitly joins the Lord's voice with the God of glory thundering. John's crowd hears the heavenly voice but divides between thunder and an angel speaking. This compares concrete divine-voice/thunder imagery without endorsing both crowd explanations as fact, inventing a storm or making the Psalm a report of this event.

Peter requests hands and head as well as feet after Jesus' no-share warning. Exodus specifies priestly hand-and-foot washing before service. Both specify bodily washing in relation to participation, but Exodus does not add head washing here, and John does not make Peter an Aaronite or impose the priestly death warning on this conversation.

Both scenes place Peter at a doorway with a female servant involved in admission. John has another disciple speak to the doorkeeper and bring him in; Acts has Rhoda recognize his voice but leave the gate shut in joy before it is opened. The women, houses and circumstances differ, and the unnamed disciple remains unnamed.

Jesus' request for newly caught fish is compared with His command to bring the available loaves and fish before feeding the crowd. The concrete food-contribution command precedes a meal in both narratives. Catch and existing supplies, disciples' breakfast and crowd feeding remain distinct; no new multiplication or identity of occasions is asserted.

In both post-resurrection exchanges, a question about the future is answered with a boundary on the disciples' concern and a task from Jesus. Peter asks about the other disciple before being told to follow; the group asks about kingdom timing before being commissioned as witnesses. Neither question is assigned an unspoken motive or its requested timetable supplied.

review_notes: All 36 saved John deferrals were reread as complete original units with neighboring context. Each has a preserved previous reason, exact source-text hash and individual new assessment. No previously completed source record is edited or recredited.

25 particular connections are proposed after reading every retained target with context; 11 cases continue deferred with zero completion credit. No source gains credit merely from previous deferral or inventory inclusion.

The review distinguishes a supported bounded comparison from independent attestation of every detail. Internal back-references, explanations, contrastive states and recurring named-participant roles are labelled as such; unrelated transitions are not used automatically to clear every remaining source.

Exact Saints words, display text, original identities, Greek-based numbering, gaps, divisions and continuation paragraphs are preserved. Targets use complete original contiguous units; no self-containing target or duplicated directed pair is retained.

Specific John comparisons preserve sea-travel observations, reported motives, differing Judea journeys and regional-origin objections; parental testimony and its limits; geographical proximity versus a Jerusalem approach; Roman political arguments; distinct priestly and requested washings; different doorway participants; different food contributions and post-resurrection questions. No absent conscience clause, unreported route or personal identity is supplied.

All 25 retained John target comparisons were independently read with their actual context in complete peer-review displays. Tested but unretained candidates are identified in the individual assessments; no global or other-book target total is used as this file's retained count.
